title: Where Python fits in data engineering
md:
By the end of this chapter you know what data engineers actually use Python for, where SQL or Spark is the better tool, and how to run every example in this handbook without installing anything. ## What the job looks like SQL moves and reshapes data that already sits in a warehouse. Python does everything around it: - **Ingestion.** Call an API, page through the results, land the raw JSON in storage. - **Glue.** Read a file from S3 or ADLS, check it, rename it, trigger the next step. - **Orchestration.** Airflow DAGs, Databricks jobs and Prefect flows are Python files. - **Transformation at scale.** PySpark is Python on top of a cluster. The syntax you learn here carries straight over. - **Quality and testing.** Validate rows, compare row counts, unit test a transform before it touches production. - **Tooling.** Small command-line tools, backfill scripts and one-off fixes that save a team hours. A useful rule: **if the data is already in a database, push the work to SQL. If you need to fetch, loop, branch, retry or call something, use Python.** Most real pipelines use both. ## Python versus the alternatives | Task | Best tool | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | Aggregate 500 million rows in a warehouse | SQL | The engine is built for it and the data never leaves | | Call a paginated REST API every hour | Python | Loops, retries and auth are natural | | Join two 2 TB datasets | PySpark or Spark SQL | Needs a cluster | | Clean a 200 MB CSV once | pandas | Fast to write, fits in memory | | Validate every file that lands in a folder | Python | Branching logic and good error messages | ## Running code in this handbook Every Python block with a **Run it** button runs right here, in your browser, using a real Python 3 interpreter (Pyodide). The first run takes a few seconds to start; after that it is instant. You can **edit any block** before running it. Blocks on a page share one Python session, like cells in a notebook, so run them top to bottom. Try it. Change the name and run it again: ```python name = "Asha" orders = [1200, 450, 3100] print(f"{name} placed {len(orders)} orders worth ₹{sum(orders):,}") ``` The last line of a block is shown automatically if it is a value, exactly like a notebook: ```python max(orders) - min(orders) ``` Blocks marked without a Run button show code that needs a real machine, such as a cloud SDK or a scheduler. ## What a small pipeline looks like Here is the shape you will build in the final chapter of this handbook: extract, validate, transform, load. Read it now and come back to it at the end. ```python raw = [ {"order_id": "1", "amount": "1200", "city": " pune "}, {"order_id": "2", "amount": "abc", "city": "Delhi"}, {"order_id": "3", "amount": "300", "city": "goa"}, ] def clean(row): return {"order_id": int(row["order_id"]), "amount": float(row["amount"]), "city": row["city"].strip().title()} good, bad = [], [] for row in raw: try: good.append(clean(row)) except ValueError as e: bad.append({**row, "error": str(e)}) print("loaded:", good) print("rejected:", bad) ``` Notice what a pipeline cares about that a coding puzzle doesn't: **bad rows are kept, not lost**, and the error says why. That habit is the difference between a script and a pipeline. ## How this handbook is organised 1. The language, fast: types, data structures, functions, strings, errors. 2. Working with data: files, CSV, JSON, dates, big files with generators. 3. Writing code a team can run: classes, decorators, logging, config, APIs. 4. pandas and databases. 5. Testing, concurrency and packaging. 6. A complete mini pipeline, then an interview playbook. ## In the interview - *"When would you use Python instead of SQL?"* Say: SQL for set-based work on data that is already in a database; Python for fetching, branching, retrying, calling services and orchestration. Then give one example from your own work. - *"Which Python libraries do you use as a data engineer?"* A strong short list: `pandas`, `pyarrow`, `requests`, `boto3` or `azure-storage-blob`, `sqlalchemy`, `pytest`, and `pyspark`. ```quiz Which job is a better fit for Python than for SQL? - Summing sales per month in a warehouse table * Calling a paginated API every hour and landing the JSON - Joining two tables that are already in the warehouse > Loops, retries and authentication are where Python shines. Set-based work on data in a database belongs to SQL. --- In this handbook, what happens when you run two blocks on the same page? * They share one Python session, so the second can use variables from the first - Each block starts a fresh Python, so nothing carries over - Only the last block on the page can be run > Blocks on a page work like notebook cells. Run them top to bottom. --- What separates a pipeline from a quick script in the example above? - It uses a for loop * Bad rows are kept with the reason they failed, instead of disappearing - It prints its output > Pipelines are judged on what happens to bad data. Silently dropping rows is the classic bug. ```

title: Python essentials, fast
md:
By the end of this chapter you can read and write everyday Python: values and types, f-strings, truthiness, `if`, loops and the few syntax rules that trip people coming from SQL or Java. ## Values and types Python figures out the type from the value. You don't declare it. ```python order_id = 1042 # int amount = 1299.50 # float city = "Pune" # str is_paid = True # bool coupon = None # "no value", like SQL NULL for v in [order_id, amount, city, is_paid, coupon]: print(repr(v), type(v).__name__) ``` `None` is Python's missing value. Test for it with `is None`, never `== None`. It reads better, and a class can redefine `==` but not `is`. ## Numbers: two traps every DE hits ```python print(7 / 2) # true division always gives a float print(7 // 2) # floor division print(7 % 2) # remainder print(0.1 + 0.2) # floats are binary fractions ``` `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`. For money, use `Decimal` (or store paise as integers). Never compare floats with `==`; check that they are close. ```python from decimal import Decimal import math print(Decimal("0.10") + Decimal("0.20")) print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)) ``` Build a `Decimal` from a **string**, not a float. `Decimal(0.1)` copies the float's error. ## Strings and f-strings f-strings are the modern way to build text. They can format numbers too: ```python customer, total, share = "Ravi", 1234567.891, 0.4567 print(f"{customer} spent ₹{total:,.2f}") # thousands separator, 2 decimals print(f"share: {share:.1%}") # as a percentage print(f"{'id':<6}|{'city':>8}|") # pad left / right in a column print(f"{total=}") # name and value, handy for debugging ``` ## Truthiness In an `if`, empty things count as false: `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `set()` and `None`. Everything else is true. ```python rows = [] if not rows: print("nothing to load, skipping") batch_size = 0 if batch_size: # careful: 0 is falsy print("never printed") if batch_size is not None: # what you usually meant print("batch size was set to", batch_size) ``` The second case is a real bug pattern. When `0` is a valid value, test `is not None`. ## Conditions and loops Indentation is the syntax. Four spaces per level. ```python amounts = [120, 0, 3400, -50, 980] for a in amounts: if a < 0: print(a, "refund") elif a == 0: print(a, "free item") elif a >= 1000: print(a, "high value") else: print(a, "normal") ``` `enumerate` gives you the index, `zip` walks lists side by side, and `range` counts: ```python cities = ["Pune", "Delhi", "Goa"] sales = [300, 500, 120] for i, (c, s) in enumerate(zip(cities, sales), start=1): print(i, c, s) total = 0 for n in range(1, 6): total += n print("1+2+3+4+5 =", total) ``` `while` loops run until a condition changes. Use `break` to leave early and `continue` to skip to the next round: ```python pages, page = [], 1 while True: if page == 3: page += 1 continue # pretend page 3 was empty pages.append(page) if page >= 5: break page += 1 print(pages) ``` ## Comparisons chain ```python age = 27 print(18 <= age < 60) # same as 18 <= age and age < 60 print("Pune" in cities) print(3 not in [1, 2]) ``` `and` and `or` short-circuit. `x or default` returns the first truthy value, which is a common way to fill a blank: ```python raw_city = "" city = raw_city or "Unknown" city ``` That trick replaces `0` too, so use it only when `0` is not a real value. ## Common mistakes - Using `== None` instead of `is None`. - `if count:` when `0` is a valid count. - Mixing tabs and spaces. Let your editor insert four spaces. - Building money with floats. Use `Decimal("12.34")` or integer paise. - Forgetting that `/` always returns a float, even `4 / 2`. ## In the interview - *"What's the difference between `is` and `==`?"* `==` compares values; `is` checks that two names point to the same object. Use `is` only for `None`, `True` and `False`. - *"Why is `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`?"* Floats are stored in binary and can't represent 0.1 exactly. Use `Decimal` for money and `math.isclose` for comparisons. - *"What is truthiness?"* Empty containers, zero and `None` are false in a condition; everything else is true. ```quiz What does `7 // 2` return? - 3.5 * 3 - 4 > `//` is floor division. `/` always returns a float. --- A function returns 0 for a valid empty batch and None when the batch failed. How do you test for failure? - if not result: * if result is None: - if result == False: > `not result` is also true for 0, so it would treat a valid empty batch as a failure. --- How should you create a Decimal for ₹19.99? * Decimal("19.99") - Decimal(19.99) - float("19.99") > Passing a float copies its binary rounding error into the Decimal. ```

title: Lists, dicts, sets and tuples
md:
By the end of this chapter you pick the right container without thinking, know what each operation costs, and write comprehensions that replace most loops. ## The four containers | Type | Looks like | Ordered | Changeable | Duplicates | Use it for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | list | `[1, 2, 2]` | yes | yes | yes | rows, a sequence of things | | tuple | `(1, "Pune")` | yes | no | yes | a fixed record, dict keys | | dict | `{"id": 1}` | insertion order | yes | keys unique | lookups by key, one row | | set | `{1, 2}` | no | yes | no | membership, de-duplication | ## Lists ```python orders = [120, 450, 3100] orders.append(75) # add to the end orders.extend([10, 20]) # add many orders.insert(0, 999) # add at a position (slow on big lists) print(orders) print(orders[0], orders[-1]) # first, last print(orders[1:3]) # slice: index 1 up to, not including, 3 print(sorted(orders, reverse=True)[:3]) # top 3 ``` `sorted()` returns a new list; `list.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`. Writing `orders = orders.sort()` is a classic bug that leaves you with `None`. ## Dicts: the workhorse A dict is one row, a lookup table, a counter, a config. Learn it well. ```python row = {"order_id": 7, "city": "Pune", "amount": 450} print(row["city"]) print(row.get("coupon")) # None instead of KeyError print(row.get("coupon", "NONE")) # with a default row["amount"] += 50 row["status"] = "paid" # add a key for key, value in row.items(): print(key, "=", value) ``` Counting and grouping come up in every pipeline. `collections` has the right tools: ```python from collections import Counter, defaultdict cities = ["Pune", "Goa", "Pune", "Delhi", "Pune", "Goa"] print(Counter(cities).most_common(2)) orders = [("Pune", 300), ("Goa", 120), ("Pune", 500)] by_city = defaultdict(list) for city, amount in orders: by_city[city].append(amount) print(dict(by_city)) print({c: sum(a) for c, a in by_city.items()}) ``` Merging dicts, newest value wins: ```python defaults = {"retries": 3, "timeout": 30} overrides = {"timeout": 60} config = defaults | overrides # Python 3.9+, same as {**defaults, **overrides} config ``` ## Sets ```python yesterday = {101, 102, 103, 104} today = {103, 104, 105} print("new:", today - yesterday) print("gone:", yesterday - today) print("still there:", today & yesterday) print("all:", today | yesterday) ``` That is a full change-detection between two snapshots in four lines. Sets also de-duplicate: `set(ids)`. If you need to keep the original order while de-duplicating, use `list(dict.fromkeys(ids))`. ## Tuples A tuple is a fixed record. Because it can't change, it can be a dict key or a set member, which a list can't. ```python point = ("Pune", "2025-12-01") daily = {point: 4200} city, day = point # unpacking print(city, day, daily[("Pune", "2025-12-01")]) ``` ## What things cost This is what interviewers mean by "time complexity" for everyday code: | Operation | list | dict / set | | --- | --- | --- | | `x in container` | O(n), scans everything | O(1) on average | | get by index / key | O(1) | O(1) | | append / add | O(1) | O(1) | | insert or delete at front | O(n) | O(1) | The single biggest speed-up in beginner pipeline code is turning a list you search repeatedly into a set or dict: ```python import time valid_ids = list(range(200_000)) incoming = list(range(0, 400_000, 7)) t = time.perf_counter() hits = sum(1 for x in incoming[:2000] if x in valid_ids) # list: scans each time slow = time.perf_counter() - t valid_set = set(valid_ids) t = time.perf_counter() hits2 = sum(1 for x in incoming if x in valid_set) # set: hash lookup fast = time.perf_counter() - t print(f"list, 2,000 lookups: {slow:.3f}s set, {len(incoming):,} lookups: {fast:.3f}s") ``` ## Comprehensions A comprehension builds a list, dict or set in one expression. Read it as "give me *this* for each item *where* condition". ```python amounts = [120, 0, 3400, -50, 980] print([a for a in amounts if a > 0]) print([a * 1.18 for a in amounts]) # add 18% GST print({a: a > 1000 for a in amounts}) # dict comprehension print({c.lower() for c in ["Pune", "PUNE", "Goa"]}) # set comprehension ``` Nested data flattens with two `for` clauses, written in the same order as the loops: ```python baskets = [["milk", "bread"], ["eggs"], ["milk", "rice"]] [item for basket in baskets for item in basket] ``` If a comprehension needs more than one `if` or gets hard to read, write the loop. Clarity wins. ## Copying: the mutable trap ```python a = [1, 2, 3] b = a # same list, two names b.append(4) print(a) import copy rows = [{"id": 1, "tags": ["x"]}] shallow = list(rows) deep = copy.deepcopy(rows) rows[0]["tags"].append("y") print(shallow[0]["tags"], deep[0]["tags"]) ``` Assignment never copies. `list(x)` or `x.copy()` copies one level; nested lists and dicts are still shared. Use `copy.deepcopy` when you need a fully separate copy. ## Common mistakes - Searching a list inside a loop. Build a set or dict once. - `x = x.sort()`. Sort returns `None`. - `row["key"]` on data you don't control. Use `.get()` with a default. - Expecting `b = a` to copy. - Using a list as a dict key. Use a tuple. ## In the interview - *"List vs tuple?"* Lists change, tuples don't; tuples can be dict keys and signal "fixed record". - *"How is a dict lookup O(1)?"* Keys are hashed to find their slot directly. That's also why keys must be immutable. - *"Remove duplicates but keep order?"* `list(dict.fromkeys(items))`. ```quiz You check 1 million incoming IDs against 200,000 valid IDs. What structure should hold the valid IDs? - A list * A set - A tuple > Membership in a set is a hash lookup, O(1) on average. A list scans every element. --- What does `orders.sort()` return? - The sorted list * None - A copy of the list > It sorts in place. Use `sorted(orders)` when you want a new list. --- Why can a tuple be a dict key but a list can't? * Tuples are immutable, so their hash can't change - Tuples are faster - Lists are not ordered > A key's hash must stay the same for its whole life. A list could change after you insert it. ```

title: Functions that a team can reuse
md:
By the end of this chapter you write small, testable functions with clear inputs and outputs, avoid the mutable-default trap, and use `*args`, `**kwargs`, type hints and `key=` functions the way production code does. ## Why functions matter in pipelines A transform you can call with sample data is a transform you can test. The goal is functions that take data in, return data out, and don't secretly change anything else. These are called *pure* functions, and they make pipelines easy to debug. ```python def add_gst(amount: float, rate: float = 0.18) -> float: """Return the amount including GST, rounded to 2 decimals.""" return round(amount * (1 + rate), 2) print(add_gst(1000)) print(add_gst(1000, rate=0.05)) ``` The `: float` and `-> float` parts are **type hints**. Python doesn't enforce them at runtime, but your editor and tools like `mypy` use them to catch mistakes, and they document the function for the next person. ## Arguments: positional, keyword, defaults ```python def load(table, rows, *, mode="append", batch_size=500): return f"{mode} {len(rows)} rows into {table} in batches of {batch_size}" print(load("orders", [1, 2, 3])) print(load("orders", [1, 2, 3], mode="overwrite")) ``` The bare `*` means everything after it must be passed by name. Use it for flags like `mode`: `load("orders", rows, "overwrite")` would be unclear, so the function forbids it. ## The mutable default trap This is the most famous Python bug, and it is asked in interviews constantly. ```python def add_tag(tag, tags=[]): # the list is created ONCE, when the function is defined tags.append(tag) return tags print(add_tag("a")) print(add_tag("b")) # surprise: the same list again ``` The fix is to default to `None` and create the list inside: ```python def add_tag(tag, tags=None): if tags is None: tags = [] tags.append(tag) return tags print(add_tag("a"), add_tag("b")) ``` ## `*args` and `**kwargs` `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; `**kwargs` collects extra named ones into a dict. You'll see them in wrappers and decorators. ```python def log_event(event, *args, **kwargs): print(event, args, kwargs) log_event("load_done", "orders", 1200, duration_s=3.2, ok=True) params = {"duration_s": 1.1, "ok": False} log_event("load_failed", **params) # unpack a dict into keyword arguments ``` ## Returning several values A function can return a tuple, and the caller unpacks it: ```python def split_valid(rows): good = [r for r in rows if r.get("amount", 0) > 0] bad = [r for r in rows if r.get("amount", 0) <= 0] return good, bad good, bad = split_valid([{"amount": 5}, {"amount": -1}, {}]) print(len(good), "good,", len(bad), "bad") ``` ## Functions are values: `key=` and lambdas You can pass a function to another function. Sorting and grouping use this all the time. ```python orders = [ {"id": 1, "city": "Pune", "amount": 300}, {"id": 2, "city": "Goa", "amount": 1200}, {"id": 3, "city": "Pune", "amount": 800}, ] by_amount = sorted(orders, key=lambda o: o["amount"], reverse=True) print([o["id"] for o in by_amount]) # sort by city, then by amount descending print([o["id"] for o in sorted(orders, key=lambda o: (o["city"], -o["amount"]))]) print(max(orders, key=lambda o: o["amount"])["id"]) ``` A `lambda` is a one-line unnamed function. If it needs more than one expression, write a normal `def`. ## Scope: where names live A name assigned inside a function is local to it. Reading an outer name works; assigning to it creates a new local. Pass values in and return them out rather than relying on globals. ```python RATE = 0.18 # a constant, fine to read anywhere def total(amount): return amount * (1 + RATE) counter = 0 def bump(): global counter # possible, but a smell in pipeline code counter += 1 bump(); bump() print(total(100), counter) ``` ## Small functions compose Here is a cleaning step built from three tiny, testable functions: ```python def strip_all(row): return {k: v.strip() if isinstance(v, str) else v for k, v in row.items()} def normalise_city(row): return {**row, "city": row["city"].title() if row.get("city") else "Unknown"} def to_paise(row): return {**row, "amount_paise": round(float(row["amount"]) * 100)} def clean(row): for step in (strip_all, normalise_city, to_paise): row = step(row) return row clean({"city": " navi mumbai ", "amount": " 12.5 "}) ``` Each step returns a new dict with `{**row, ...}` instead of changing the input. If a step fails, the original row is still intact for the error report. ## Common mistakes - Mutable defaults like `def f(x=[])` or `def f(cfg={})`. - Functions that both change their input and return it. Pick one, preferably return a new value. - Long functions that read files, transform and write. Split I/O from logic so the logic can be tested. - Using `global` to pass data around. ## In the interview - *"What's wrong with `def f(items=[])`?"* The default list is created once and shared between calls. Use `None` and create it inside. - *"What are `*args` and `**kwargs`?"* Extra positional arguments as a tuple and extra keyword arguments as a dict. Used for wrappers and flexible APIs. - *"What is a pure function and why do data engineers care?"* Same input, same output, no side effects. It can be unit tested with sample data and re-run safely. ```quiz What does `add_tag("b")` return after `add_tag("a")` if the function is `def add_tag(t, tags=[]): tags.append(t); return tags`? - ['b'] * ['a', 'b'] - An error > The default list is created once when the function is defined and is shared across calls. --- In `def load(table, rows, *, mode="append")`, what does the bare `*` do? * Forces `mode` to be passed by name - Collects extra positional arguments - Makes `mode` required > Everything after a bare `*` is keyword-only. --- How do you sort a list of dicts by amount, largest first? - sorted(orders, reverse=True) * sorted(orders, key=lambda o: o["amount"], reverse=True) - orders.sort("amount") > `key=` tells sort what to compare. Dicts themselves can't be compared. ```

title: Strings and cleaning text
md:
By the end of this chapter you can clean messy text fields the way real source systems deliver them: stray spaces, mixed case, odd separators, phone numbers in five formats, and values hidden inside free text. ## The everyday methods ```python raw = " Navi MUMBAI , MH " print(repr(raw.strip())) # trim both ends print(raw.strip().lower()) print(raw.strip().title()) print(raw.split(",")) # split on a separator print([p.strip() for p in raw.split(",")]) print(" | ".join(["Pune", "Goa", "Delhi"])) print("ORD-1042".startswith("ORD-"), "report.csv".endswith((".csv", ".tsv"))) print("ORD-1042".removeprefix("ORD-")) # Python 3.9+ print("a,b,,c".replace(",,", ",")) ``` Strings never change in place. Every method returns a new string, so remember to assign the result: `name = name.strip()`. ## Checking what a string contains ```python for s in ["1042", "12.5", "-3", "abc", "", "٣"]: print(repr(s), s.isdigit(), s.isdecimal()) ``` `isdigit()` says nothing about decimals or negatives, and it accepts digits from other scripts. To check "is this a number", try to convert it: ```python def to_float(s): try: return float(s) except (TypeError, ValueError): return None [to_float(x) for x in ["12.5", "-3", "1e3", "abc", None, " 7 "]] ``` ## Slicing ```python code = "IN-MH-PUNE-411001" print(code[:2], code[-6:], code[3:5]) print(code[::-1]) # reversed print(code.split("-")[2]) ``` ## Regular expressions When the pattern is more complex than a fixed separator, use `re`. Learn five pieces and you can read most patterns: `\d` digit, `\w` letter or digit, `\s` whitespace, `+` one or more, `( )` capture. ```python import re text = "Order #1042 paid ₹1,299.50 on 2025-12-03; order #1043 failed" print(re.findall(r"#(\d+)", text)) # all order numbers print(re.search(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", text).groups()) print(re.sub(r"[₹,]", "", "₹1,299.50")) # drop currency and commas ``` Always write patterns as raw strings, `r"..."`, so backslashes reach `re` untouched. ### Normalise phone numbers Real data mixes formats. Strip everything that isn't a digit, then apply rules: ```python def clean_phone(raw): if not raw: return None digits = re.sub(r"\D", "", raw) # \D = anything that isn't a digit if len(digits) == 12 and digits.startswith("91"): digits = digits[2:] if len(digits) == 11 and digits.startswith("0"): digits = digits[1:] return digits if len(digits) == 10 and digits[0] in "6789" else None for p in ["+91 98765-43210", "098765 43210", "9876543210", "12345", None, "(022) 2345 6789"]: print(repr(p), "->", clean_phone(p)) ``` Notice the last one: a landline with an area code doesn't pass the mobile rule, so it becomes `None` rather than a wrong number. In a real pipeline you'd send it to a reject table with the reason. ### Named groups for readable parsing ```python line = '10.0.0.7 - - [03/Dec/2025:10:15:32 +0530] "GET /api/orders HTTP/1.1" 503 512' pattern = re.compile(r'(?P\S+) .*?\[(?P[^\]]+)\] "(?P\w+) (?P\S+)[^"]*" (?P\d{3})') m = pattern.match(line) m.groupdict() ``` `re.compile` once and reuse the pattern inside loops. It saves re-parsing the pattern on every line. ## Unicode and invisible characters Data from spreadsheets and web forms carries characters you can't see: non-breaking spaces, zero-width spaces, curly quotes. They make `"Pune" != "Pune"`. ```python import unicodedata a = "Pune " # non-breaking space at the end b = "Pune" print(a == b, a.strip() == b) # strip() does handle   c = "Pu​ne" # zero-width space in the middle print(c == b, len(c)) def normalise(s): s = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", s) s = re.sub(r"[​-‍﻿]", "", s) # zero-width characters and BOM return " ".join(s.split()) # collapse all runs of whitespace print(normalise(c) == b, repr(normalise(" “Navi  Mumbai” "))) ``` `" ".join(s.split())` is a neat idiom: `split()` with no argument splits on any whitespace and drops empties, so joining back collapses every run to a single space. ## Common mistakes - Forgetting to assign: `name.strip()` alone does nothing. - Using `isdigit()` to validate numbers. Try the conversion instead. - Regex without `r"..."`. - Treating a failed clean as a valid value. Return `None` and record why. - Comparing text without normalising case, spaces and Unicode first. ## In the interview - *"How do you clean a column of phone numbers?"* Remove non-digits, strip known country or trunk prefixes, validate length and leading digit, send failures to a reject table with a reason. - *"Why are two strings that look equal not equal?"* Hidden characters: non-breaking or zero-width spaces, different Unicode forms, trailing whitespace. Normalise with `unicodedata.normalize` and collapse whitespace. ```quiz What does `" a b ".split()` return? - ['', 'a', 'b', ''] * ['a', 'b'] - [' a b '] > With no argument, split() splits on any run of whitespace and drops empty pieces. --- Why write regex patterns as r"\d+" instead of "\d+"? * So Python passes backslashes to the regex engine unchanged - It makes the regex faster - Raw strings ignore case > In a normal string, sequences like \b or \n would be turned into special characters first. --- "12.5".isdigit() returns? - True * False - 12.5 > The dot isn't a digit. To check for a number, try float() and catch ValueError. ```
Practise thisPython 3Palindrome check ignoring case, spaces and punctuationPython 11Character with the longest consecutive run (earliest on ties)Python 13Top 3 most common words, case-insensitive, ignoring punctuationPython 16First non-repeating character in a string, in O(n)Python 33Parse web logs: count 5xx errors per IP

title: Errors, exceptions and failing well
md:
By the end of this chapter you handle errors on purpose: catch only what you expect, keep bad records with a reason, raise clear errors of your own, and retry the failures that are worth retrying. ## Reading a traceback When something fails, Python prints a traceback. Read it **from the bottom**: the last line is the error type and message, and the line above it is where it happened. ```python def parse_amount(s): return float(s) try: parse_amount("₹1,200") except ValueError as e: print(type(e).__name__, "->", e) ``` ## try, except, else, finally ```python def safe_divide(a, b): try: result = a / b except ZeroDivisionError: print("b was zero, returning None") return None else: # runs only if nothing failed print("ok") return result finally: # always runs: close files, release locks, log timing print("done", a, b) safe_divide(10, 2) safe_divide(1, 0) ``` ## Catch narrowly Catch only the errors you expect and know how to handle. A bare `except:` or `except Exception:` around everything hides real bugs, like a typo in a variable name. ```python rows = [{"amount": "10"}, {"amount": "x"}, {}] for r in rows: try: print(float(r["amount"])) except ValueError: print("not a number:", r) except KeyError: print("missing amount:", r) ``` ## Keep bad records, don't lose them The pipeline pattern: every row ends up in exactly one place, good or rejected, and rejected rows carry the reason. ```python def validate(row): if not row.get("order_id"): raise ValueError("missing order_id") amount = float(row["amount"]) # may raise ValueError itself if amount < 0: raise ValueError(f"negative amount {amount}") return {"order_id": int(row["order_id"]), "amount": amount} source = [ {"order_id": "1", "amount": "250"}, {"order_id": "", "amount": "99"}, {"order_id": "3", "amount": "-5"}, {"order_id": "4", "amount": "abc"}, ] good, rejects = [], [] for i, row in enumerate(source, start=1): try: good.append(validate(row)) except ValueError as e: rejects.append({"line": i, "row": row, "reason": str(e)}) print(f"{len(good)} good, {len(rejects)} rejected") for r in rejects: print(r) assert len(good) + len(rejects) == len(source) # nothing silently lost ``` That last `assert` is a reconciliation check. Put one at the end of every load: rows in must equal rows out plus rows rejected. ## Raising your own errors Raise early, with a message that tells the reader what to do. ```python class DataContractError(Exception): """The source broke the agreed schema.""" def check_columns(header, required=("order_id", "amount", "order_ts")): missing = [c for c in required if c not in header] if missing: raise DataContractError(f"source file is missing columns {missing}; got {header}") try: check_columns(["order_id", "amt", "order_ts"]) except DataContractError as e: print("stop the load:", e) ``` A custom exception lets callers treat "the source broke the contract" differently from "the network blipped". ## Chaining: keep the original cause ```python def read_config(text): import json try: return json.loads(text) except json.JSONDecodeError as e: raise ValueError("config file is not valid JSON") from e try: read_config("{bad json") except ValueError as e: print(e, "| caused by:", repr(e.__cause__)) ``` `raise ... from e` keeps the low-level error attached, so the traceback shows both. ## Retry what is worth retrying Network timeouts and rate limits are *transient*: trying again later usually works. Bad data is not; retrying won't fix it. Retry with exponential backoff and a cap: ```python import random, time class TransientError(Exception): pass calls = {"n": 0} def flaky_api(): calls["n"] += 1 if calls["n"] < 3: raise TransientError("503 Service Unavailable") return {"rows": 42} def with_retry(fn, attempts=5, base=0.05): for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1): try: return fn() except TransientError as e: if attempt == attempts: raise wait = base * 2 ** (attempt - 1) * (1 + random.random() * 0.1) print(f"attempt {attempt} failed ({e}); retrying in {wait:.2f}s") time.sleep(wait) with_retry(flaky_api) ``` The small random part, called *jitter*, stops many workers retrying at exactly the same moment. Chapter 12 turns this into a reusable decorator. ## Common mistakes - `except:` or `except Exception:` around a whole job, which swallows real bugs. - Logging an error and carrying on as if the row loaded. - Retrying bad data. Only retry transient failures. - Raising `Exception("error")` with no useful message. - `return` inside `finally`, which silently cancels an exception. ## In the interview - *"How do you handle bad records in a pipeline?"* Validate each row, route failures to a reject table or dead-letter queue with the reason and source line, reconcile counts at the end, and alert if the reject rate passes a threshold. - *"Which errors do you retry?"* Transient ones: timeouts, 429 and 5xx responses, connection resets. Use exponential backoff with jitter and a maximum number of attempts. Never retry 4xx validation errors or bad data. - *"What does `finally` do?"* Runs whether or not an exception happened. Use it, or a `with` block, to release resources. ```quiz Where do you start reading a Python traceback? * At the bottom: the error type and message, then the line above it - At the top: the first function called - In the middle > The last line names the error, and the frame just above it is where it was raised. --- Which failure should a pipeline retry? - A row with amount "abc" * An HTTP 503 from the source API - A file missing a required column > 503 is transient. Bad data and contract breaks will fail again on every retry. --- What does `raise ValueError("...") from e` do? - Ignores e * Raises the new error and keeps e attached as its cause - Re-raises e unchanged > The traceback shows both errors, so you keep the low-level detail. ```

title: Files, paths and CSV
md:
By the end of this chapter you read and write files safely with `with` and `pathlib`, handle CSV files the way real sources send them (quotes, commas inside values, odd encodings), and land output atomically so a crash never leaves a half-written file. The examples write small files into the in-browser file system, so you can run them freely. ## Paths with pathlib `pathlib.Path` replaces string juggling with `os.path`. Paths join with `/` and know their own parts. ```python from pathlib import Path base = Path("data") landing = base / "landing" / "2025-12-03" landing.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) f = landing / "orders_001.csv" print(f) print(f.name, f.stem, f.suffix, f.parent.name) print(f.with_suffix(".parquet").name) ``` ## Reading and writing text Always open files with `with`. It closes the file even if an error happens halfway. ```python f.write_text("order_id,city,amount\n1,Pune,250\n2,Goa,1200\n", encoding="utf-8") with open(f, encoding="utf-8") as fh: for line_no, line in enumerate(fh, start=1): print(line_no, line.rstrip("\n")) ``` Iterating over the file object reads one line at a time, so even a 20 GB file uses almost no memory. `fh.read()` loads the whole file; only do that for small files. Always pass `encoding="utf-8"`. Without it, Python uses the machine's default, which differs between Windows and Linux, and a job that works on your laptop fails on the server. ## Listing files ```python for i in range(3): (landing / f"orders_{i:03}.csv").write_text("order_id,amount\n1,10\n", encoding="utf-8") (landing / "_SUCCESS").write_text("", encoding="utf-8") csvs = sorted(landing.glob("*.csv")) print([p.name for p in csvs]) print("ready to load:", (landing / "_SUCCESS").exists()) ``` Many systems write a `_SUCCESS` marker when a folder is complete. Check for it before loading, or you may read a folder that is still being written. ## CSV: never split on commas yourself Real CSV files have commas inside quoted values, quotes inside values, and line breaks inside cells. `line.split(",")` breaks on all of them. The `csv` module handles them correctly. ```python import csv messy = Path("data/messy.csv") messy.write_text( 'order_id,customer,address,amount\n' '1,"Rao, Asha","12 MG Road, Pune",250\n' '2,"Khan ""Bunty"" Imran","Flat 4\nBandra",1200\n' '3,Meera,Goa,\n', encoding="utf-8", ) with open(messy, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh: for row in csv.DictReader(fh): print(row) ``` Two details matter: `newline=""` lets the `csv` module handle line endings inside quoted cells, and `DictReader` gives each row as a dict keyed by the header. Notice row 3: a missing value arrives as an empty string `''`, not `None`. Convert it yourself. ## Writing CSV ```python rows = [ {"order_id": 1, "city": "Pune", "note": 'said "call first"'}, {"order_id": 2, "city": "Navi Mumbai, MH", "note": ""}, ] out = Path("data/out.csv") with open(out, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh: w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=["order_id", "city", "note"]) w.writeheader() w.writerows(rows) print(out.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) ``` The writer quotes values that contain commas or quotes for you. ## Encodings and the Excel BOM Files exported from Excel often start with an invisible byte-order mark, so your first column is called `'﻿order_id'` instead of `'order_id'`, and lookups fail. Read such files with `encoding="utf-8-sig"`, which drops the BOM: ```python bom = Path("data/excel_export.csv") bom.write_bytes("﻿order_id,amount\n1,10\n".encode("utf-8")) with open(bom, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh: print(next(csv.reader(fh))) with open(bom, newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as fh: print(next(csv.reader(fh))) ``` Older Indian government and bank files sometimes arrive in `cp1252` or `latin-1`. If a UTF-8 read fails with `UnicodeDecodeError`, ask the source for the encoding rather than guessing; `errors="replace"` hides the problem by turning bad bytes into `�`. ## Write atomically If a job crashes while writing `report.csv`, readers may pick up a half-written file. Write to a temporary name in the same folder, then rename. A rename within one file system is atomic: readers see the old file or the new one, never half. ```python import os, tempfile def write_atomic(path: Path, text: str): path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, prefix=".tmp_", suffix=path.suffix) try: with os.fdopen(fd, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh: fh.write(text) os.replace(tmp, path) # atomic swap except BaseException: os.remove(tmp) raise write_atomic(Path("data/gold/daily_sales.csv"), "day,revenue\n2025-12-03,48210\n") print(Path("data/gold/daily_sales.csv").read_text()) ``` Object stores like S3 and ADLS don't have a real rename, but the same idea applies: write to a staging prefix, then publish by writing a manifest or `_SUCCESS` marker last. ## Common mistakes - `line.split(",")` on CSV. Use the `csv` module. - Opening without `encoding="utf-8"`. - Forgetting `newline=""` with the `csv` module. - Reading a landing folder before its `_SUCCESS` marker exists. - Writing the final file directly, so a crash leaves a partial file. ## In the interview - *"How would you read a 30 GB CSV on a laptop with 8 GB RAM?"* Stream it: iterate over the file or `csv.reader` row by row, or read in chunks with pandas `chunksize`, and aggregate as you go. Never load it whole. - *"How do you make sure downstream jobs don't read a half-written file?"* Write to a temp name and rename atomically, or publish a `_SUCCESS` marker or manifest last, and have readers wait for it. ```quiz Why use the csv module instead of line.split(",")? * Quoted values can contain commas, quotes and line breaks - split() is slower - csv.reader converts types automatically > The csv module follows the quoting rules. It does not convert types; every value is a string. --- Your first column comes back as '﻿order_id'. What fixes it? - strip() on every row * Open the file with encoding="utf-8-sig" - Open with errors="ignore" > That's a byte-order mark from Excel. utf-8-sig removes it. --- Why write to a temp file and then os.replace() it? - It is faster * Readers never see a half-written file - It compresses the file > A rename within one file system is atomic. ```

title: JSON and nested data
md:
By the end of this chapter you parse API payloads safely, flatten nested JSON into table rows, explode arrays, and stream JSON Lines files that are too big to load at once. ## JSON in, Python out ```python import json payload = '{"order_id": 7, "paid": true, "coupon": null, "items": [{"sku": "A1", "qty": 2}]}' order = json.loads(payload) print(order) print(type(order["paid"]), order["coupon"]) print(json.dumps(order, indent=2)) ``` JSON maps to Python like this: object → `dict`, array → `list`, `true`/`false` → `True`/`False`, `null` → `None`. Numbers become `int` or `float`. `json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False)` keeps text like "₹" or "मुंबई" readable instead of escaping it. ## Read nested values safely APIs leave fields out. Chained `[]` access fails on the first missing key. Write a small helper: ```python event = {"user": {"id": 42, "address": {"city": "Pune"}}, "device": None} def dig(obj, *path, default=None): for key in path: if isinstance(obj, dict) and key in obj: obj = obj[key] elif isinstance(obj, list) and isinstance(key, int) and -len(obj) <= key < len(obj): obj = obj[key] else: return default return obj print(dig(event, "user", "address", "city")) print(dig(event, "user", "address", "pin", default="UNKNOWN")) print(dig(event, "device", "os")) ``` ## Flatten nested objects into columns Warehouses want flat rows. Join nested keys with dots or underscores: ```python def flatten(obj, parent="", sep="."): out = {} for k, v in obj.items(): key = f"{parent}{sep}{k}" if parent else k if isinstance(v, dict): out.update(flatten(v, key, sep)) else: out[key] = v return out flatten({"id": 1, "user": {"id": 42, "address": {"city": "Pune", "pin": "411001"}}, "tags": ["new"]}) ``` Lists are left alone on purpose. A list of child records is a separate table, not extra columns. ## Explode arrays into child rows One order with three items becomes three rows in an `order_items` table, each carrying the parent key: ```python orders = [ {"order_id": 1, "city": "Pune", "items": [{"sku": "A1", "qty": 2, "price": 120}, {"sku": "B7", "qty": 1, "price": 999}]}, {"order_id": 2, "city": "Goa", "items": []}, {"order_id": 3, "city": "Delhi"}, ] order_rows, item_rows = [], [] for o in orders: order_rows.append({"order_id": o["order_id"], "city": o["city"], "item_count": len(o.get("items") or [])}) for line_no, item in enumerate(o.get("items") or [], start=1): item_rows.append({"order_id": o["order_id"], "line_no": line_no, **item}) print(order_rows) print(item_rows) ``` Orders 2 and 3 have no items, but they still appear in `order_rows`. Exploding without keeping the parent row is how orders silently disappear from reports. Spark calls these two behaviours `explode` and `explode_outer`. ## JSON Lines: one record per line Event exports and log files usually use JSON Lines (`.jsonl`): one JSON object per line. You can stream them line by line and skip a broken line instead of failing the whole file. ```python from pathlib import Path Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True) Path("data/events.jsonl").write_text( '{"event": "view", "user": 1}\n' '{"event": "cart", "user": 1}\n' '{"event": "view", "user": 2\n' # broken line '\n' '{"event": "buy", "user": 1}\n', encoding="utf-8", ) good, bad = [], [] with open("data/events.jsonl", encoding="utf-8") as fh: for n, line in enumerate(fh, start=1): if not line.strip(): continue try: good.append(json.loads(line)) except json.JSONDecodeError as e: bad.append((n, str(e))) print(len(good), "events;", "bad lines:", bad) ``` Writing JSON Lines is just `fh.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")` per record. ## Dates and decimals don't serialise by default ```python from datetime import datetime, date from decimal import Decimal rec = {"ts": datetime(2025, 12, 3, 10, 15), "day": date(2025, 12, 3), "amount": Decimal("12.50")} def to_json(o): if isinstance(o, (datetime, date)): return o.isoformat() if isinstance(o, Decimal): return str(o) # keep exact value as text raise TypeError(f"can't serialise {type(o).__name__}") json.dumps(rec, default=to_json) ``` ## Schema drift Sources add, rename and drop fields without telling you. Compare each record's keys against what you expect: ```python EXPECTED = {"order_id", "city", "amount"} def drift(record): keys = set(record) return {"missing": sorted(EXPECTED - keys), "new": sorted(keys - EXPECTED)} print(drift({"order_id": 1, "city": "Pune", "amount": 10})) print(drift({"order_id": 2, "city_name": "Goa", "amount": 5, "channel": "app"})) ``` New fields are usually safe to keep in a raw JSON column. Missing required fields should stop the load or go to rejects. ## Common mistakes - `data["a"]["b"]["c"]` on API data. Fields go missing. - Exploding child arrays and dropping parents that have none. - Loading a huge `.json` array whole. Ask for JSON Lines, or stream. - Storing money as float after parsing. Use `json.loads(s, parse_float=Decimal)` when exactness matters. ## In the interview - *"How would you load nested JSON into a warehouse?"* Land it raw first. Then flatten scalar fields into columns, explode arrays into child tables keyed by the parent id, keep the full payload in a JSON column for fields you don't model yet, and track schema drift. - *"Why JSON Lines over one big JSON array?"* It streams line by line, appends cheaply, splits for parallel processing, and one bad line doesn't break the whole file. ```quiz An order has an empty items list. When you explode items into order_items, what must you make sure of? - Skip the order entirely * The order still appears in the orders table - Insert a fake item > Dropping parents with no children is how orders vanish from reports. Keep the parent row. --- What does json.loads turn `null` into? - "null" - 0 * None > JSON null maps to Python None. --- Why is JSON Lines easier to process than one large JSON array? * Each line is a complete record, so you can stream and skip bad lines - It is always smaller - It supports more data types > You never need the whole file in memory, and one broken line doesn't stop the load. ```

title: Dates, times and time zones
md:
By the end of this chapter you parse timestamps from messy sources, store everything in UTC, convert to IST only for display, and avoid the off-by-one-day bugs that break daily reports. ## The golden rule **Store and compute in UTC. Convert to local time only at the edges**, when you read a local value in or show a value to a person. Mixing time zones inside a pipeline is the most common cause of "yesterday's numbers changed". ## naive versus aware A *naive* datetime has no time zone; it is just a wall-clock reading. An *aware* datetime knows its offset from UTC. Only aware values can be compared safely across sources. ```python from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo IST = ZoneInfo("Asia/Kolkata") naive = datetime(2025, 12, 3, 23, 30) aware_ist = datetime(2025, 12, 3, 23, 30, tzinfo=IST) aware_utc = aware_ist.astimezone(timezone.utc) print(naive, naive.tzinfo) print(aware_ist) print(aware_utc) ``` 11:30 pm in Pune on 3 December is 6:00 pm UTC the same day. Now take 2:00 am IST on 4 December: in UTC it is still 3 December. A report that groups by UTC date puts that order on the 3rd, while the business thinks it happened on the 4th. Decide which "day" the report means, write it down, and convert before grouping. ```python late_night = datetime(2025, 12, 4, 2, 0, tzinfo=IST) print("IST day:", late_night.date(), "| UTC day:", late_night.astimezone(timezone.utc).date()) ``` ## Parsing what sources send ISO 8601 strings parse directly: ```python print(datetime.fromisoformat("2025-12-03T10:15:00+05:30")) print(datetime.fromisoformat("2025-12-03T04:45:00Z")) # Z means UTC, accepted since Python 3.11 print(datetime.fromisoformat("2025-12-03")) ``` Other formats need a pattern. `%d/%m/%Y` is the Indian style; `%m/%d/%Y` is American. "03/12/2025" means 3 December in one and 12 March in the other, so never guess: agree the format with the source. ```python print(datetime.strptime("03/12/2025 18:05", "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M")) print(datetime.strptime("03-Dec-2025", "%d-%b-%Y").date()) print(datetime.strptime("20251203", "%Y%m%d").date()) ``` Unix epoch timestamps are seconds (or milliseconds) since 1 January 1970 UTC: ```python epoch_ms = 1764756000000 print(datetime.fromtimestamp(epoch_ms / 1000, tz=timezone.utc)) ``` Always pass `tz=timezone.utc`. Without it you get local time of whatever server runs the job. ### A tolerant parser that never guesses silently ```python FORMATS = ["%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M", "%Y-%m-%d"] def parse_ts(s, assume_tz=IST): s = (s or "").strip().replace("Z", "+00:00") for fmt in FORMATS: try: dt = datetime.strptime(s, fmt) except ValueError: continue if dt.tzinfo is None: dt = dt.replace(tzinfo=assume_tz) # a documented assumption, not a guess return dt.astimezone(timezone.utc) raise ValueError(f"unrecognised timestamp {s!r}") for s in ["2025-12-03T10:15:00+0530", "2025-12-03 10:15:00", "03/12/2025 10:15", "2025-12-03", "yesterday"]: try: print(f"{s!r:30} -> {parse_ts(s)}") except ValueError as e: print(e) ``` ## Arithmetic with timedelta ```python now = datetime(2025, 12, 3, 10, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc) print(now + timedelta(days=7)) print(now - timedelta(hours=36)) print((datetime(2025, 12, 31, tzinfo=timezone.utc) - now).days, "days to year end") ``` ## Windows for incremental loads Daily jobs process a half-open window `[start, end)`: start included, end excluded. Then consecutive windows never overlap and never miss a row. ```python from datetime import date def day_window(d: date, tz=IST): start = datetime(d.year, d.month, d.day, tzinfo=tz) end = start + timedelta(days=1) return start.astimezone(timezone.utc), end.astimezone(timezone.utc) s, e = day_window(date(2025, 12, 3)) print(f"WHERE order_ts >= '{s.isoformat()}' AND order_ts < '{e.isoformat()}'") ``` Using `BETWEEN '2025-12-03 00:00' AND '2025-12-03 23:59:59'` loses anything in the last second and double-counts rows at midnight across two days. The half-open window is always right. ## Formatting for people ```python ts = datetime(2025, 12, 3, 18, 5, tzinfo=timezone.utc).astimezone(IST) print(ts.strftime("%d %b %Y, %I:%M %p IST")) print(ts.isoformat(timespec="seconds")) ``` Use ISO 8601 (`isoformat()`) for anything a machine reads: logs, files, APIs. ## Common mistakes - `datetime.now()` without a time zone. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. - Grouping by UTC date when the business means the IST day. - `BETWEEN` with `23:59:59` for daily windows. Use `>= start AND < end`. - Guessing between dd/mm and mm/dd. - Comparing naive and aware datetimes, which raises `TypeError`, or worse, comparing two naive values from different zones, which silently gives the wrong answer. ## In the interview - *"How do you handle time zones in a pipeline?"* Convert to UTC on ingestion, store UTC, compute in UTC, and convert to the business time zone only for day boundaries and display. Document which time zone defines a reporting day. - *"An order at 1 am IST shows on the wrong day. Why?"* The report groups by UTC date; 1 am IST is the previous day in UTC. Convert to IST before taking the date. - *"How do you define a daily incremental window?"* Half-open: `ts >= day_start AND ts < next_day_start`, with both bounds computed in the business time zone and converted to UTC. ```quiz An order is placed at 02:00 IST on 4 December. What is its UTC date? * 3 December - 4 December - 5 December > IST is UTC+5:30, so 02:00 IST is 20:30 UTC on the previous day. --- Which filter correctly selects one day of orders? - order_ts BETWEEN '2025-12-03 00:00:00' AND '2025-12-03 23:59:59' * order_ts >= '2025-12-03 00:00:00' AND order_ts < '2025-12-04 00:00:00' - DATE(order_ts) = '2025-12-03' using the server's local time > A half-open window never misses the last fraction of a second and never overlaps the next day. --- What should you pass to datetime.fromtimestamp for epoch values from an API? - Nothing * tz=timezone.utc - tz=ZoneInfo("Asia/Kolkata") always > Without tz you get the server's local time, which changes from machine to machine. ```

title: Generators and processing big files
md:
By the end of this chapter you process data that doesn't fit in memory: stream records with generators, batch them for loading, and build lazy pipelines that read, clean and write in one pass using almost no RAM. ## Lists hold everything; generators hold one thing A list comprehension builds every element at once. A **generator** produces one element at a time, only when asked. ```python import sys squares_list = [n * n for n in range(1_000_000)] squares_gen = (n * n for n in range(1_000_000)) # round brackets: a generator expression print(f"list: {sys.getsizeof(squares_list):,} bytes") print(f"generator: {sys.getsizeof(squares_gen):,} bytes") print(sum(squares_gen)) ``` The generator is a couple of hundred bytes, whatever its length. The trade-off: you can loop over it only once. ```python g = (x for x in [1, 2, 3]) print(list(g), list(g)) # the second list is empty: g is used up ``` ## Writing a generator function with yield Any function with `yield` becomes a generator. It pauses at each `yield` and continues from there next time. ```python def read_records(path): """Yield one cleaned dict per line, skipping blanks and comments.""" with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as fh: for line in fh: line = line.strip() if not line or line.startswith("#"): continue order_id, city, amount = line.split("|") yield {"order_id": int(order_id), "city": city, "amount": float(amount)} from pathlib import Path Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True) Path("data/orders.psv").write_text("# id|city|amount\n1|Pune|250\n\n2|Goa|1200\n3|Pune|80\n", encoding="utf-8") for rec in read_records("data/orders.psv"): print(rec) ``` The file stays open only while you are iterating, and the `with` block closes it when the generator finishes. ## Lazy pipelines: chain generators Each stage takes an iterable and yields results. Nothing runs until the last stage pulls data through. ```python def only_valid(records): for r in records: if r["amount"] > 0: yield r def add_gst(records, rate=0.18): for r in records: yield {**r, "amount_with_gst": round(r["amount"] * (1 + rate), 2)} pipeline = add_gst(only_valid(read_records("data/orders.psv"))) print(pipeline) # nothing has run yet print(list(pipeline)) ``` This is exactly how Spark thinks: transformations are lazy, and an action like `count()` or `write` triggers the work. ## Generate a big file, then aggregate it in constant memory Let's write half a million lines, then total revenue per city while holding only one line at a time. ```python import random, time random.seed(7) cities = ["Pune", "Goa", "Delhi", "Mumbai", "Chennai"] t = time.perf_counter() with open("data/big_orders.psv", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh: for i in range(1, 500_001): fh.write(f"{i}|{random.choice(cities)}|{random.randint(50, 5000)}\n") print(f"wrote 500k rows in {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s, {Path('data/big_orders.psv').stat().st_size / 1e6:.0f} MB") ``` ```python from collections import Counter t = time.perf_counter() revenue = Counter() for rec in read_records("data/big_orders.psv"): revenue[rec["city"]] += rec["amount"] print({c: f"{v:,.0f}" for c, v in revenue.most_common()}) print(f"aggregated in {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s") ``` Memory use stays flat no matter how big the file gets. This is the answer to "count records per key in a 50 GB file on an 8 GB machine". ## Batching for loads Databases and APIs prefer batches: one insert of 1,000 rows is far faster than 1,000 inserts. `itertools.islice` takes the next *n* items from any iterator: ```python from itertools import islice def batched(iterable, size): it = iter(iterable) while batch := list(islice(it, size)): yield batch for b in batched(range(1, 11), 4): print(b) ``` Python 3.12 added `itertools.batched`, which does the same and returns tuples. The version above works everywhere and shows the idea. ```python loaded = 0 for batch in batched(read_records("data/big_orders.psv"), 50_000): loaded += len(batch) # here you'd call executemany() or a bulk API print(f"{loaded:,} rows loaded in {loaded // 50_000} batches") ``` ## Useful itertools ```python from itertools import chain, groupby, accumulate print(list(chain([1, 2], [3], [4, 5]))) # read several files as one stream print(list(accumulate([100, 250, 50]))) # running total rows = sorted([("Pune", 10), ("Goa", 5), ("Pune", 7)], key=lambda r: r[0]) for city, group in groupby(rows, key=lambda r: r[0]): # input must be sorted by the key print(city, sum(v for _, v in group)) ``` `groupby` only groups *consecutive* equal keys, like a sorted-merge. Forgetting to sort first is a classic bug. ## Common mistakes - `list(huge_generator)` "just to check", which loads everything. - Looping over a used-up generator a second time and getting nothing. - `groupby` on unsorted data. - Opening a file in a generator and never finishing the loop. The file stays open until the generator is garbage collected; call `.close()` on it or loop to the end. ## In the interview - *"Count records per key in a 50 GB log on an 8 GB machine."* Stream it line by line with a generator and keep a `Counter` of keys. If the number of distinct keys itself is too large, hash-partition into smaller files first, then count each. - *"Generator vs list?"* A list stores all items and can be reused; a generator yields items lazily, uses constant memory and can be consumed once. - *"How do you load 10 million rows into a database efficiently from Python?"* Stream and batch, use bulk APIs (`executemany`, `COPY`, or the warehouse's bulk loader), commit per batch, and make it restartable. ```quiz What is printed by `g = (x for x in [1, 2]); print(list(g), list(g))`? - [1, 2] [1, 2] * [1, 2] [] - An error > A generator can only be consumed once. --- Why does `itertools.groupby` need sorted input? * It only groups consecutive items with the same key - It sorts internally but slowly - It raises an error otherwise > Unsorted input gives several separate groups for the same key. --- Which approach totals revenue per city in a 50 GB file with 8 GB of RAM? - Read the file with .read() and split lines * Iterate line by line and add to a Counter - Load it into a list of dicts first > Streaming keeps one line in memory at a time. ```

title: Classes and dataclasses
md:
By the end of this chapter you know when a class earns its place in pipeline code, model records with `@dataclass`, and write a small class that holds configuration and state for a job. ## When to write a class Most transformation code is best as plain functions. A class helps when you have **data and behaviour that belong together and some state that lives across calls**: a database connection with a retry policy, a job that tracks its own metrics, a reader that remembers where it stopped. ## Dataclasses: records with less typing `@dataclass` writes the boring parts (`__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`) for you. ```python from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict from datetime import date @dataclass class Order: order_id: int city: str amount: float tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list) # never a bare [] default day: date = date(2025, 12, 3) o = Order(1, "Pune", 250.0) print(o) print(o == Order(1, "Pune", 250.0)) print(asdict(o)) ``` `field(default_factory=list)` is the dataclass version of the mutable-default fix from chapter 4. ## Validate on creation `__post_init__` runs after the generated `__init__`. Put checks there, and a bad record can't even be created. ```python @dataclass(frozen=True) # frozen: fields can't be changed after creation class Payment: payment_id: str amount_paise: int currency: str = "INR" def __post_init__(self): if self.amount_paise < 0: raise ValueError(f"{self.payment_id}: negative amount") if self.currency not in {"INR", "USD"}: raise ValueError(f"{self.payment_id}: unknown currency {self.currency}") @property def rupees(self) -> float: return self.amount_paise / 100 p = Payment("P1", 129950) print(p.rupees) try: Payment("P2", -5) except ValueError as e: print("rejected:", e) try: p.amount_paise = 1 except Exception as e: print(type(e).__name__, "- frozen records can't be edited") ``` Frozen dataclasses are hashable, so they can live in sets and be dict keys, which is handy for de-duplication. ## A small class with state Here is a job that tracks its own counts, so the final log line and the reconciliation check come for free: ```python import time class LoadJob: def __init__(self, name: str, reject_limit: float = 0.05): self.name = name self.reject_limit = reject_limit self.read = self.loaded = self.rejected = 0 self.errors: list[str] = [] self._t0 = time.perf_counter() def process(self, rows, transform): for row in rows: self.read += 1 try: transform(row) self.loaded += 1 except (ValueError, KeyError) as e: self.rejected += 1 self.errors.append(f"row {self.read}: {e}") return self def finish(self): took = time.perf_counter() - self._t0 assert self.read == self.loaded + self.rejected, "rows went missing" rate = self.rejected / self.read if self.read else 0 status = "FAILED" if rate > self.reject_limit else "OK" return f"[{status}] {self.name}: read={self.read} loaded={self.loaded} rejected={self.rejected} ({rate:.0%}) in {took:.3f}s" def __repr__(self): return f"LoadJob({self.name!r}, read={self.read})" job = LoadJob("orders_daily").process( [{"amount": "10"}, {"amount": "x"}, {"amount": "30"}, {}], lambda r: float(r["amount"]), ) print(job) print(job.finish()) print(job.errors) ``` `self` is the object itself. Attributes set on `self` in `__init__` live as long as the object. A leading underscore, as in `_t0`, tells other developers "internal, don't touch". ## Inheritance, briefly Inheritance lets a class reuse another's behaviour. In data code, the most useful form is a common interface with several implementations: ```python class Sink: def write(self, rows): raise NotImplementedError class PrintSink(Sink): def write(self, rows): for r in rows: print("PRINT", r) class MemorySink(Sink): def __init__(self): self.rows = [] def write(self, rows): self.rows.extend(rows) def run(rows, sink: Sink): sink.write([r for r in rows if r["ok"]]) data = [{"id": 1, "ok": True}, {"id": 2, "ok": False}] run(data, PrintSink()) mem = MemorySink(); run(data, mem); print("memory sink holds", mem.rows) ``` The pipeline doesn't care where data goes. In production, `Sink` might be S3, a warehouse table or Kafka; in tests, it's `MemorySink`. Keep hierarchies shallow; one level is usually enough. ## Common mistakes - A class for everything. If it has one method and no state, make it a function. - Mutable defaults in dataclasses. Use `field(default_factory=...)`. - Validation scattered around the code instead of in `__post_init__`. - Deep inheritance trees nobody can follow. ## In the interview - *"Why use a dataclass?"* Less boilerplate for record types, readable `repr`, equality by value, optional immutability with `frozen=True`, and type hints that document the schema. - *"What's `self`?"* The instance the method was called on. Python passes it automatically. - *"How would you make a pipeline easy to test?"* Depend on an interface such as `Sink`, inject the real implementation in production and an in-memory one in tests. ```quiz How do you give a dataclass field an empty list as its default? - tags: list = [] * tags: list = field(default_factory=list) - tags: list = None and never fix it > A bare [] default would be shared by every instance; dataclasses refuse it. --- What does frozen=True do on a dataclass? * Prevents changing fields after creation and makes instances hashable - Makes it faster to create - Stops it being printed > Frozen instances can go into sets and be dict keys. --- When is a class better than a function in pipeline code? - Always - Never * When data and behaviour belong together and state lives across calls > A job that tracks counts or a client that keeps a connection are good examples. ```

title: Decorators and context managers
md:
By the end of this chapter you can read and write decorators for timing, retries and logging, and write context managers that always clean up, which covers two of the most asked Python interview questions for data engineers. ## Functions that wrap functions A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one that adds behaviour around it. `@timed` above a function is shorthand for `fn = timed(fn)`. ```python import functools, time def timed(fn): @functools.wraps(fn) # keep the original name and docstring def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): t0 = time.perf_counter() try: return fn(*args, **kwargs) finally: print(f"{fn.__name__} took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.4f}s") return wrapper @timed def transform(rows): """Square every value.""" return [r * r for r in rows] print(transform(list(range(100_000)))[-1]) print(transform.__name__, "-", transform.__doc__) ``` Without `functools.wraps`, every decorated function would be called `wrapper`, which makes logs and tracebacks useless. ## A retry decorator with arguments To pass settings, add one more layer: a function that takes the settings and returns the decorator. ```python import random def retry(attempts=3, base_delay=0.05, on=(Exception,)): def decorator(fn): @functools.wraps(fn) def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1): try: return fn(*args, **kwargs) except on as e: if attempt == attempts: raise delay = base_delay * 2 ** (attempt - 1) + random.uniform(0, base_delay) print(f"{fn.__name__}: attempt {attempt} failed with {e!r}, sleeping {delay:.2f}s") time.sleep(delay) return wrapper return decorator state = {"calls": 0} @retry(attempts=4, on=(ConnectionError, TimeoutError)) def fetch_page(page): state["calls"] += 1 if state["calls"] < 3: raise ConnectionError("connection reset") return {"page": page, "rows": 100} print(fetch_page(1)) ``` Note `on=`: the decorator retries only the errors you list. A `KeyError` from a bug passes straight through instead of being retried four times. ## Caching `functools.lru_cache` remembers results for arguments it has seen. Great for slow, repeatable lookups such as fetching a currency rate for a day: ```python @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1024) def fx_rate(day: str, currency: str) -> float: time.sleep(0.05) # pretend this calls an API return {"USD": 83.2, "EUR": 90.1}[currency] t0 = time.perf_counter() for _ in range(50): fx_rate("2025-12-03", "USD") print(f"50 calls in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s;", fx_rate.cache_info()) ``` Only cache pure functions whose answer can't change for the same inputs. ## Context managers: setup and guaranteed cleanup You already use one: `with open(...)`. A context manager runs setup when the block starts and cleanup when it ends, even if the block raises. The quickest way to write one is `contextlib.contextmanager`. Code before `yield` is setup, code after is cleanup: ```python from contextlib import contextmanager @contextmanager def step(name): t0 = time.perf_counter() print(f"▶ {name}") try: yield except Exception as e: print(f"✖ {name} failed: {e}") raise finally: print(f"■ {name} finished in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.3f}s") with step("extract"): data = list(range(10)) try: with step("load"): raise RuntimeError("warehouse unavailable") except RuntimeError: pass ``` ### A transaction-style context manager Commit on success, roll back on any error. This is how database libraries implement `with conn:`. ```python class FakeTable: def __init__(self): self.rows, self._pending = [], [] @contextmanager def transaction(self): self._pending = [] try: yield self._pending self.rows.extend(self._pending) # commit print("committed", len(self._pending)) except Exception as e: print("rolled back:", e) raise finally: self._pending = [] t = FakeTable() with t.transaction() as tx: tx.extend([1, 2, 3]) try: with t.transaction() as tx: tx.append(4) raise ValueError("bad row") except ValueError: pass print("table:", t.rows) ``` The failed batch leaves no trace in the table. That is exactly the behaviour you want from a load step. ### The class form A class with `__enter__` and `__exit__` does the same. Returning `True` from `__exit__` would swallow the exception, which you almost never want. ```python class Timer: def __enter__(self): self.t0 = time.perf_counter() return self def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb): self.seconds = time.perf_counter() - self.t0 return False # don't hide errors with Timer() as t: sum(range(1_000_000)) print(f"{t.seconds:.4f}s") ``` ## Common mistakes - Forgetting `functools.wraps`. - A retry decorator that retries every exception, including your own bugs. - `lru_cache` on a function whose result changes over time, such as "latest orders". - Cleanup code after `yield` without `try/finally`, so it is skipped on error. - Returning `True` from `__exit__` by accident and hiding exceptions. ## In the interview - *"Write a retry decorator with exponential backoff."* Outer function takes settings, middle takes the function, inner wrapper loops over attempts, catches only listed exceptions, sleeps `base * 2 ** attempt` plus jitter, re-raises on the last attempt, and uses `functools.wraps`. - *"Write a context manager that times a block."* Either `@contextmanager` with `try/yield/finally`, or a class with `__enter__` and `__exit__`. - *"Where would you use a context manager in a pipeline?"* Files, DB connections and transactions, locks, temporary directories, and timing or logging around a step. ```quiz What does functools.wraps do in a decorator? * Copies the wrapped function's name and docstring onto the wrapper - Makes the function run faster - Adds retry behaviour > Without it every decorated function shows up as "wrapper" in logs and tracebacks. --- In a @contextmanager function, where does cleanup code go so it runs even if the block fails? - Before yield * In a finally after yield - In a separate function > Wrap yield in try/finally, or an exception skips the cleanup. --- Which errors should a retry decorator retry? - All exceptions * Only the transient ones you list, like ConnectionError or TimeoutError - Only KeyError > Retrying your own bugs or bad data just fails slower. ```

title: Logging and configuration
md:
By the end of this chapter your pipeline tells you what it did, when, and why it failed, and its settings live outside the code so the same script runs in dev and prod. ## Why print() is not enough `print` has no level, no timestamp, no idea which module spoke, and you can't turn it down in production. The `logging` module gives you all of that from the standard library. ```python import logging, sys logging.basicConfig( level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)-7s %(name)s | %(message)s", datefmt="%H:%M:%S", stream=sys.stdout, force=True, # replace any earlier setup (handy in notebooks) ) log = logging.getLogger("orders_etl") log.debug("not shown: below INFO") log.info("extract started, source=%s", "s3://raw/orders/2025-12-03") log.warning("3 rows had a null customer_id, sent to quarantine") log.error("load failed: %s", "warehouse timeout") ``` Use one logger per module with `logging.getLogger(__name__)`. Pass values as arguments (`"%s", value`) rather than f-strings, so the string is only built when the message is actually emitted. ## Levels, and what goes where | Level | Use it for | |---|---| | DEBUG | Row-level detail you only want while fixing something | | INFO | Step started or finished, row counts, file names | | WARNING | Something odd but handled: quarantined rows, a retry | | ERROR | A step failed | | CRITICAL | The whole job can't continue | A good pipeline log reads like a story: what came in, what was dropped and why, what went out. ## Logging exceptions with the traceback Inside an `except`, `log.exception` logs at ERROR and attaches the traceback for you. ```python def parse_amount(raw): return float(raw) for raw in ["12.5", "abc", "7"]: try: parse_amount(raw) except ValueError: log.exception("bad amount %r", raw) ``` ## Structured (JSON) logs Log platforms such as Datadog, CloudWatch or Azure Monitor search JSON far better than free text. A small formatter turns every record into one JSON line: ```python import json, time class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter): def format(self, record): payload = { "ts": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S", time.gmtime(record.created)), "level": record.levelname, "logger": record.name, "msg": record.getMessage(), } payload.update(getattr(record, "ctx", {})) # extra fields return json.dumps(payload) handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout) handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter()) jlog = logging.getLogger("orders_etl.json") jlog.handlers = [handler] jlog.propagate = False # don't print twice jlog.setLevel(logging.INFO) jlog.info("load finished", extra={"ctx": {"run_id": "r-481", "rows": 12_408, "table": "silver.orders"}}) ``` Now you can search "every run where rows was 0" instead of grepping text. ## Configuration: keep settings out of the code Hard-coded paths and passwords are the classic beginner smell. Settings usually come from three places, in this order of priority: 1. Environment variables (secrets, and anything that differs per environment) 2. A config file in the repo (defaults that rarely change) 3. Defaults in the code ```python import os from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass(frozen=True) class Settings: env: str source_path: str batch_size: int db_password: str | None def load_settings(file_cfg: dict) -> Settings: env = os.environ.get("APP_ENV", "dev") cfg = {**file_cfg.get("default", {}), **file_cfg.get(env, {})} return Settings( env=env, source_path=os.environ.get("SOURCE_PATH", cfg["source_path"]), batch_size=int(os.environ.get("BATCH_SIZE", cfg.get("batch_size", 1000))), db_password=os.environ.get("DB_PASSWORD"), # never in the file ) file_cfg = { # what you'd read from config.toml "default": {"source_path": "data/raw", "batch_size": 500}, "prod": {"source_path": "s3://raw/orders"}, } print(load_settings(file_cfg)) os.environ["APP_ENV"] = "prod" os.environ["BATCH_SIZE"] = "5000" print(load_settings(file_cfg)) ``` Note `int(...)`: environment variables are always strings. Forgetting to convert them is a common bug. ### Reading a TOML file Python 3.11+ ships `tomllib`, so a config file needs no extra package. ```python import tomllib text = """ [default] source_path = "data/raw" batch_size = 500 [prod] source_path = "s3://raw/orders" """ with open("config.toml", "w") as f: f.write(text) with open("config.toml", "rb") as f: # tomllib wants bytes file_cfg = tomllib.load(f) print(file_cfg["prod"]) ``` ### Fail fast on bad config Check settings once at start-up, not halfway through a three-hour job. ```python def validate(s: Settings): problems = [] if s.batch_size <= 0: problems.append("batch_size must be positive") if s.env == "prod" and not s.db_password: problems.append("DB_PASSWORD is required in prod") if problems: raise SystemExit("config error: " + "; ".join(problems)) try: validate(load_settings(file_cfg)) except SystemExit as e: print(e) ``` ## Common mistakes - `print` in production code, so nothing has a level or timestamp. - Building log messages with f-strings at DEBUG level in a hot loop. - Logging secrets, full rows with personal data, or tokens. - Treating `os.environ["X"]` as an int without converting it. - Passwords in a committed config file. Use environment variables or a secrets manager. - Calling `basicConfig` in a library module. Only the entry-point script configures logging. ## In the interview - *"How do you make a pipeline observable?"* Structured logs with a run id, row counts in and out per step, warnings for quarantined data, errors with tracebacks, and metrics or alerts on top of those logs. - *"How do you handle config across dev, test and prod?"* One code base, settings from environment variables layered over a config file, secrets from a secrets manager, validated at start-up. ```quiz Inside an except block, which call logs the error together with its traceback? - log.info(e) * log.exception("message") - print(traceback) > log.exception logs at ERROR level and attaches the current traceback. --- os.environ.get("BATCH_SIZE") returns "5000". What type is that? - int * str - float > Environment variables are always strings, so convert them. --- Where should a database password live? - In config.toml committed to git - Hard-coded as a default * In an environment variable or secrets manager > Anything in git is effectively public to everyone with repo access, forever. ```
